article.title: India's regional dishes: food stories served, not written
article.desc: From a grandmother's dal to your city's famous street snack, India's food heritage lives on the table, not in books. How to discover, cook and share the dishes of every region.
article.intro: India's greatest food stories were never written down. They were served: passed from one kitchen to the next, one festival to the next, one generation to the next. Every state, and often every street, has a dish that tells you exactly where you are.

sections.h: Recipes that live at the table
sections.p: Many family recipes survive only because someone cooked them beside a parent or grandparent. The measurements were a handful, a pinch, until it smells right. When that cook is gone, the recipe can go too, unless someone has learned it by doing.

sections.h: Learn by sharing, not just reading
sections.p: Tradition thrives when it is shared, not just told. Cook one family dish with the person who knows it best, film the steps on your phone, and serve it to friends who have never tried it. Food knowledge travels fastest hand to hand.

sections.h: Taste your way across the map
sections.p: Start with the dish your own city is famous for, then pick one from a state you have never visited: a coastal curry, a hill-country bread, a street snack from another metro. Regional food is the easiest way to travel without leaving the table.

sections.h: The pairing that completes the plate
sections.p: Hot, spicy and fried food loves contrast. A cold, crisp cola cuts through the heat and resets the palate between bites, which is why bold Indian flavours and a chilled Pepsi have shared the table for so long.

article.close: Order the dish your city is famous for tonight, and tell us your state's dish.

persona.t: Aria is the Culinary Voyager — street food, regional discovery and food-travel nostalgia, 71 posts and 10% of creator content. She is the explorer who carries the heritage pillar from one table to the next.

pain.t: Creators put 47% of their Foodie content into India's food heritage while every cola is absent — and the category's own pairing content decayed from 34% to 0%, verified. That is WHITESPACE: claim it.

angle.t: Social learning says traditions pass on by doing, not telling — and this is the most-reacted lane in the creator panel, with 2.9M engagement on 324 posts. Creators already teach food culture by sharing it.

insight.t: Pepsi is not borrowing this story — it has decades of meal-pairing equity, 125 years in India and chilled availability at the meal. Sharing tradition at the table is a lane it once ran and can re-enter.

ship.t: This pillar takes 50% of the calendar and leads the quarter. Let TOFU tell the table's story, MOFU prove the crisp carbonation built to cut through spice, and BOFU add a chilled Pepsi to tonight's order.

a2.s: Cognitive dissonance is the pull between treat and health. Aria's pain is heritage people never got to learn.
a2.t: Cognitive dissonance explains the discomfort of wanting a treat while trying to eat well, and the urge to settle that clash. Aria's pain isn't an inner tug-of-war; it's that India's culinary heritage has gaps in awareness and accessibility, so many people never get to know these dishes at all. Look for a lens about how food know-how travels from one person to the next when people cook, eat and share together.

a3.s: Nostalgia works on memories people already hold. Aria's pain is heritage many have never had the chance to know.
a3.t: Nostalgia theory explains how memories of home and familiar dishes pull on the choices we make today. That needs memories to draw on, and Aria's pain is the opposite: gaps in awareness and accessibility mean many people have never tasted or learned this culinary heritage in the first place. Look for a lens about how traditions get passed on by doing them alongside someone, rather than by remembering them.

article.title: Balance without boredom: enjoy food and eat mindfully
article.desc: You want the feast and the fitness plan. How to drop the food guilt, make swaps you barely notice and build a table where nothing is forbidden and everything is chosen.
article.intro: You want the party and the plan. The biryani and the morning run. For many food lovers, the hardest part of eating well is not the food itself. It is the guilt that sits between indulgence and health.

sections.h: Why the guilt gets in the way
sections.p: Psychologists call it cognitive dissonance: the discomfort of holding two goals that seem to clash. When every treat feels like a failure, we swing between strict rules and giving up. Neither lasts.

sections.h: Health is not the enemy of indulgence
sections.p: Balance isn't a diet. It is a table where nothing is forbidden and everything is chosen. Plan the meals you love, enjoy them fully, and balance the rest of the day with lighter plates, movement and water.

sections.h: Small swaps that keep the flavour
sections.p: The swaps that stick are the ones you barely notice: grilled instead of fried for one dish, an extra helping of vegetables, a smaller second serving, or the zero-sugar version of the drink you already love.

sections.h: Make the easy choice the default
sections.p: Stock your kitchen and your weekly order with the options you actually want to choose. When the better choice is already in the fridge, balance stops being a decision you have to make at every meal.

article.close: Add Pepsi Zero Sugar to this week's order: all the Pepsi taste, none of the sugar.

angle.t: Cognitive dissonance is the itch of wanting the treat while trying to eat well. A behavioural-economic angle eases it without a lecture — when Vikram does not have to choose, the dilemma loses its grip.

insight.t: The balance story holds because Pepsi can prove it: Pepsi Black / Zero Sugar is on shelf nationwide, the product-true answer to mindful choices. Indulgence and health really can share the table.

ship.t: This pillar carries 30% of the calendar, led by an Instagram Reel. TOFU reframes balance as choice, MOFU lands all the taste with none of the sugar, and BOFU makes Zero Sugar the easy add to this week's order.

a1.s: Social learning explains how habits pass on by doing. Vikram knows food; his pain is a treat-versus-health tug.
a1.t: Social learning theory explains how people pick up traditions and habits by watching others and joining in. Vikram doesn't need teaching — he already loves great food and watches what he eats, and his pain is the tug between indulgence and health when the enjoyment turns competitive. Look for a lens about the inner discomfort of holding two wants at once, and how easing it means he no longer has to choose.

a3.s: Nostalgia links food to memories of home. Vikram's pain is a live pull between indulgence and health, not the past.
a3.t: Nostalgia theory explains how memories of home and the dishes we grew up with shape what we reach for today. Vikram's tension is happening right now: balancing indulgence and health in the middle of competitive enjoyment, where a fond memory won't quiet the wish to treat himself while eating well. Look for a lens about the mental itch of two wants pulling against each other, and how to dissolve it without a lecture.

article.title: Festive food traditions: bring back the dishes you grew up with
article.desc: A festival is a menu with a memory. How to recreate childhood festive dishes, plan one table for a scattered family and make the season taste like home again.
article.intro: A festival is a menu with a memory. One bite of a sweet you only eat once a year can take you straight back to a crowded kitchen, a grandparent's voice and a table that never seemed to empty.

sections.h: Why festive food feels like home
sections.p: Nostalgia ties memories to taste and smell more tightly than almost anything else. That is why the dishes of Onam, Dussehra or Diwali matter as much as the lights. They are how families remember who they are.
Pick one dish from your earliest festivals and recreate it this season. Call the relative who used to make it, ask for the steps, and cook it together over a video call if you live apart.

Families are spread across cities and countries, and festivals are short. Plan the menu early, share the cooking, and keep one moment when everyone, at the table or on a screen, eats the same dish at the same time.
Heavy, rich festive food needs something crisp and cold between bites. Get sharing packs into the fridge before the guests arrive, so the table is ready the moment the celebration starts.

article.close: Recreate one childhood festival dish this season. Pair it, post it, tag @pepsiindia.

Reva isn't short of that knowledge — she's a creator who lives for culture, food and festivities, and her pain is navigating celebrations and the choices they bring, where feeling counts for more than instruction. Look for a lens about the emotional pull of the past, and how it draws people back to childhood dishes when a festival comes round.

a2.t: Cognitive dissonance explains the unease of holding two conflicting wants, like craving a treat while trying to eat well.
